propositions.text: Chief Heron filed a motion under Rule 397(1)(b) for reconsideration of the Order granted in Heron v Salt River First Nation No 195, 2024 FC 413.
propositions.quote: On March 21, 2024, Cecilia (Toni) Josephine Heron [Chief Heron or Applicant] filed a motion pursuant to Rule 397(1)(b) of the Federal Court Rules, SOR/98-106 [Rules] for reconsideration in relation to the Order granted in Heron v Salt River First Nation No 195, 2024 FC 413 [Judgment].

paragraphs.summary: Applicant filed a motion for reconsideration under Rule 397(1)(b) of the Federal Court Rules regarding a prior Order.

propositions.text: The procedural background is set out in the prior Judgment.
propositions.quote: The procedural background to this matter is set forth in the Judgment.

paragraphs.summary: The procedural background is set out in the prior Judgment, stated by the court.

propositions.text: On March 12, 2024, the Court dismissed T-2191-22, allowed T-2206-22, awarded Chief Heron salary and $12,000 costs.
propositions.quote: On March 12, 2024 the Court rendered the Judgment, ordering as follows: The application for judicial review in T-2191-22 is dismissed. The application for judicial review in T-2206-22 is allowed. Chief Heron is awarded remuneration for the salary she would have received had she not been suspended. Chief Heron is awarded lump sum costs in the amount of $12,000 payable by SRFN forthwith.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismissed one application, allowed another, awarded salary and costs to Chief Heron.

propositions.text: Chief Heron requests reconsideration under Rule 397(1)(b) to declare suspensions no longer in effect and confirm her as acting Chief.
propositions.quote: Chief Heron requests that the Court reconsider the Judgment concerning T-2206-22 in accordance with Rule 397(1)(b). In the Notice of Motion, Chief Heron seeks the following relief: 1. A Declaration pursuant to Rule 397[1](b) that the relief sought in the Applicant’s judicial review for [applications] T-2206-22 and T-97-22 is hereby granted, including that this Court’s Decision rendered on March 12, 2024, held that: a) The initial October 13, 2022, suspension of Chief Heron by the Respondent, Salt River First Nation (“SRFN”) is no longer in effect. b) The subsequent suspensions by SRFN as against Chief Heron, including the suspension issued February 1, 2024 by SRFN, suspending Chief Toni Heron, for a further 60 days are no longer in effect. c)That as of the Court’s Decision on March 12, 2024, Chief Toni Heron is the acting Chief of SRFN. Costs on a solicitor-client basis; Such further and other relief as counsel may advise and this Honourable Court deems just.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks reconsideration to declare suspensions ended and confirm her as acting Chief, plus costs and other relief.

propositions.text: Chief Heron filed an affidavit about events after the hearing and Judgment, including SRFN's view on suspension and Election Code compliance.
propositions.quote: In support of this motion, Chief Heron filed an affidavit dated March 20, 2024 in which she provides evidence about events since the Court heard the underlying judicial review and since the Court rendered its Judgment on March 12, 2024. Chief Heron details how SRFN maintains the view that the Applicant remained suspended until April 4, 2023 and other concerns about whether SRFN is complying with its Election Code.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant filed affidavit about post-hearing events and SRFN's position on suspension and Election Code.

propositions.text: SRFN argues the affidavit is irrelevant and inadmissible in Rule 397 motion; reconsideration only reviews if Judgment accords with reasons.
propositions.quote: SRFN submits that the Court should disregard this evidence, as it is irrelevant and inadmissible in a Rule 397 motion. In a reconsideration under Rule 397(1), the Court being functus officio is only asking itself whether the Judgment does or does not accord with its reasons (Sharma v Canada (Revenue Agency), 2020 FCA 203 at para 3). Further, paragraphs 2 to 20 of the affidavit of Chief Heron is not relevant to the underlying judicial reviews. Evidence that is not relevant and admissible, as defined by the Applicant’s Notices of Application, has no place in a motion to reconsider the Court’s Judgment.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues affidavit is irrelevant and inadmissible; reconsideration only checks if Judgment accords with reasons.

propositions.text: Affidavit is largely irrelevant; Rule 397 addresses overlooked or omitted matters; some affidavit parts do not assist reconsideration.
propositions.quote: I agree that the affidavit of Chief Heron is largely irrelevant to this motion. Rule 397 is technical rule designed to address situations where a matter that should have been addressed was overlooked or accidentally omitted (Lee v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2003 FC 867 at para 3). Paragraphs 1 and 2 of the affidavit are introductory and summarize the Judgment. Paragraphs 3 to 14 detail events since the hearing and Judgment and have some bearing on understanding why the Applicant has filed this motion but ultimately do not assist the Court in assessing whether it overlooked or omitted a matter. In contrast, paragraphs 15 to 20 of the affidavit focusing on Chief Heron’s concerns about SRFN’s alleged contraventions of its Election Code do not relate to whether this Court overlooked or omitted a matter in its Judgment.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds affidavit largely irrelevant; Rule 397 covers overlooked or omitted matters; some affidavit parts unhelpful.

propositions.text: The sole issue is whether the Court should reconsider its relief under Rule 397(1)(b).
propositions.quote: The sole issue for determination is whether the Court should reconsider its relief ordered in its Judgment under paragraph 397(1)(b) of the Rules.

paragraphs.summary: Court states sole issue is whether to reconsider relief under Rule 397(1)(b).

propositions.text: Rule 397 allows reconsideration within 10 days for overlooked matters or inconsistencies, and correction of clerical errors.
propositions.quote: Rule 397 enables the Court to reconsider its Order: Motion to reconsider 397 (1) Within 10 days after the making of an order, or within such other time as the Court may allow, a party may serve and file a notice of motion to request that the Court, as constituted at the time the order was made, reconsider its terms on the ground that (a) the order does not accord with any reasons given for it; or (b) a matter that should have been dealt with has been overlooked or accidentally omitted. Mistakes (2) Clerical mistakes, errors or omissions in an order may at any time be corrected by the Court.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Rule 397 allows reconsideration for overlooked matters or inconsistencies and clerical error correction.

propositions.text: Chief Heron sought judicial review of SRFN Council's decision to suspend her for 60 days and ongoing extensions.
propositions.quote: In the Notice of Application for T-97-23, Chief Heron sought judicial review of the following decision: … the decision of the Council of the Salt River First Nation No. 195 (“SRFN”) wherein they decided to suspend (or extend the prior suspension of) the Applicant from her position of Chief of the SRFN for a period of 60 days, and the ongoing course of conduct of continuing to maintain and/or extend the suspension going forward (the “Decision”). The Decision was communicated to the Applicant on December 12, 2022. [emphasis added.]

paragraphs.summary: Applicant sought judicial review of SRFN Council's decision to suspend her and ongoing extensions.

propositions.text: The Notice of Application identified the ongoing extensions as the 'course of conduct' challenged.
propositions.quote: Similarly, the Notice of Application for T-97-23 identified that “[t]his conduct of repeatedly extending the suspension for a further 60 days, including the Second Suspension, is the “course of conduct” that the Applicant seeks to challenge in this application”.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant's Notice identified ongoing suspension extensions as the challenged course of conduct.

propositions.text: Chief Heron is not seeking to amend the Notice; it already addresses ongoing suspensions, consistent with Respondent's understanding.
propositions.quote: As such, Chief Heron is not seeking to amend the Notice of Application as it already addresses ongoing suspensions and a continuing course of conduct. This understanding of the decision that was under review is consistent with the Respondent’s own understanding in its memorandum of fact and law for the underlying judicial review, which stated: SRFN also opposes the request of the suspended Chief in Application No. T-97-23 (since consolidated with Application No. T-2206-22) for an Order in the nature of certiorari, quashing and setting aside SRFN Council’s December 4, 2022 and all later decisions extending the October 13 Suspension for a further 60 days without pay (“the Suspension Extensions”).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says Notice already covers ongoing suspensions; Respondent's memorandum agrees.

propositions.text: Chief Heron sought relief including prohibition of repeated suspensions and declaration she remains Chief.
propositions.quote: In her applications, Chief Heron sought relief that included an Order in the nature of prohibition restraining Council from their conduct of repeatedly suspending Chief Heron for the same allegations, as well as an Order or Declaration that Chief Heron remains the Chief.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant sought relief prohibiting repeated suspensions and declaring her as Chief.

propositions.text: Chief Heron was successful; suspensions after Sept 13, 2023 hearing are on same grounds but SRFN still claims suspension as of Feb 1, 2024.
propositions.quote: Chief Heron was entirely successful in her application. The suspensions after the September 13, 2023 hearing are on the same grounds as the grounds that were before the Court in Chief Heron’s application for T-2206-22 and T-97-23. However, SRFN continues to take the position that Chief Heron remains suspended pursuant to SRFN’s decision on February 1, 2024 to suspend her for another 60 days.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant was successful; suspensions after hearing same grounds but SRFN claims suspension continues.

propositions.text: To give effect to Judgment, Court must prohibit SRFN from continuing suspensions and confirm Chief Heron as Chief.
propositions.quote: In order to give effect to the Judgment, the Court must reconsider its Judgment to include an Order that SRFN is prohibited from continuing to suspend Chief Heron for the same grounds and that Chief Heron remains the Chief of SRFN. Otherwise, SRFN will continue to suspend Chief Heron on the same grounds and Chief Heron’s only recourse would be to file another judicial review. Chief Heron’s motion must be granted to provide certainty and finality to the Court’s Judgment.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Court must prohibit further suspensions and confirm her as Chief to give effect to Judgment.

propositions.text: Judgment needs wording confirming relief granted, including quashing all suspensions and confirming Chief Heron as Chief.
propositions.quote: The Judgment requires wording identifying that the Court granted the relief sought. In particular, the request for an Order in the nature of certiorari quashing and setting aside the decision must include the first suspension and all subsequent suspensions. It would serve everyone if the Judgment clearly stated that Chief Heron is Chief. The Judgment also requires wording that Chief Heron cannot continue to be suspended on the same grounds. Finally, the Judgment only refers to salary and not remuneration but it is possible that there is other remuneration owed to her.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says Judgment should clearly state relief granted, quash all suspensions, confirm Chief Heron as Chief, and address remuneration.

propositions.text: Rule 397 exceptions are narrow; reconsideration power is limited to correcting oversights or inconsistencies, not appeals.
propositions.quote: The exceptions to the doctrine of functus officio created by Rule 397 are “much narrower than it sounds” (Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2022 FC 8 at para 4 [Singh], citing Canada v MacDonald, 2021 FCA 6). Singh at paragraph 5 similarly identifies the following limitation, citing Yeager v Day, 2013 FCA 258: The reconsideration power under Rule 397 is not the same as this Court’s powers on appeal under section 52 of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7. Instead, the reconsideration power is more limited – to correct small oversights, such as an inconsistency between the order and the reasons (Rule 397(1)(a)), the failure of the Court to deal with something that was put to it (Rule 397(1)(b)), and clerical mistakes, errors or omissions in the order (Rule 397(2)).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Rule 397 exceptions are narrow; reconsideration is limited to correcting oversights, not appeals.

propositions.text: No clerical error exists; Judgment and Reasons are consistent and allow Chief Heron's application.
propositions.quote: There is no clerical error at issue. The Court’s Judgment and Reasons are also consistent, as the Judgment allowed Chief Heron’s application and is entirely in accordance with the Reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent says no clerical error; Judgment and Reasons consistent and allow Chief Herer's application.

propositions.text: At hearing, suspensions before Court were October 2022, December 2022, February 2023, March 2023, June 2023, and August 2023.
propositions.quote: At the time of the hearing, the suspensions before the Court were the October 2022, December 2022, February 2023, March 2023, June 2023, and August 2023 suspensions.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent states suspensions before Court at hearing were from Oct 2022 to Aug 2023.

propositions.text: This motion attempts to amend Notices and add relief not pleaded; such amendment not allowed after judgment.
propositions.quote: This motion is an attempt to amend the Notices of Application and add further relief that was not pleaded, and was not before the Court on September 13, 2023. A motion to amend does not fall within motion the very narrow exceptions to the doctrine of functus officio created by Rule 397. A Notice of Application cannot be amended retroactively. As Justice Pelletier said in Halford v Seed Hawk Inc, 2004 FC 455 [Halford]: [16] In my view, a trial judge has a broad discretion to allow amendments to the pleadings at any time prior to judgment, but that right is extinguished after judgment has been signed. At that point, there has been a final adjudication of the parties' rights which can only be attacked upon appeal. I would therefore dismiss the application for reconsideration.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues motion seeks impermissible amendment after judgment; such amendments are barred post-judgment.

propositions.text: Chief Heron's relief request in September 2023 did not include the February 1, 2024 suspension, which requires a motion to amend pleadings.
propositions.quote: Chief Heron is asking for express relief to cover the February 1, 2024 suspension so it is a motion to amend pleadings and add further relief that was not before the Court at the hearing.

propositions.text: The Court can only clarify it quashed suspensions before the hearing, not the February 1, 2024 suspension.
propositions.quote: The Court can only clarify that it quashed the October 2022, December 2022, February 2023, March 2023, June 2023, and August 2023 suspensions, which were the suspensions before the Court at the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Chief Heron's February 1, 2024 suspension relief request requires amended pleadings and the court only quashed suspensions before the hearing.

propositions.text: Rule 397(1)(a) allows reconsideration only of remedies sought, not arguments raised before the Court.
propositions.quote: the “matter” that Rule 397(1)(a) permits the Court to reconsider "is related to the remedies sought by the moving party. It is not related to an argument that was raised before the Court" (Singh at para 9, citing Naboulsi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 357).

propositions.text: Applicant's request is outside the narrow exception to functus officio under Rule 397(2).
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s request falls well outside the narrow exception to the doctrine of functus officio created by Rule 397(2) (Halford at paras 9, 10, 13, 14; Singh at para 9).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Rule 397 limits reconsideration to remedies, and finds the applicant's request outside the functus officio exception.

propositions.text: Chief Heron's relief does not fall within Rule 397 exceptions.
propositions.quote: The relief sought by Chief Heron does not fall within the exceptions of Rule 397.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Chief Heron's relief request is not within Rule 397 exceptions.

propositions.text: Court can review continuing conduct under Rule 302, not just single decisions (David Suzuki Foundation case).
propositions.quote: There is an exception to Rule 302 in which a Court can review a continuing course of conduct rather than limit the judicial review to a review of a single decision (David Suzuki Foundation v Canada (Health), 2018 FC 380 at para 164).

propositions.text: T-97-23 Notice identified continuing conduct, allowing review of suspensions up to August 2023.
propositions.quote: The wording of the T-97-23 Notice of Application identified the continuing course of conduct at issue, which is why the subsequent suspensions after the December 2022 suspension up until the August 2023 suspension were reviewable before the Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Rule 302 allows review of continuing conduct, and the T-97-23 Notice covered suspensions up to August 2023.

propositions.text: Court noted SRFN continued suspensions every 60 days after hearing but did not consider them in Judgment.
propositions.quote: While the Court identified the fact in its Reasons that SRFN continued to suspend Chief Heron every 60 days after the hearing, the Judgment did not take into consideration these suspensions as they occurred after the hearing.

propositions.text: Court cannot review decisions not before it, including February 1, 2024 suspension without pleadings or evidence.
propositions.quote: The Court cannot review a decision that is not before it. The Court did not have the benefit of pleadings or even copies of any suspensions after the hearing and so cannot rule that the February 1, 2024 suspension is no longer in effect.

propositions.text: Reasonableness of February 1, 2024 suspension may be questioned but not on Rule 397 motion.
propositions.quote: Its reasonableness may be called into question, but it is not for the Court on a Rule 397 motion to determine.

propositions.text: Chief Heron has not shown any matter was overlooked or omitted.
propositions.quote: Chief Heron has not shown that a matter that should have been dealt with has been overlooked or accidentally omitted.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it cannot review suspensions after hearing, including February 1, 2024, and Chief Heron showed no overlooked matter.

propositions.text: SRFN's conduct is abuse of process, continuing suspension despite court judgment.
propositions.quote: SRFN’s conduct is a classic abuse of process (Toronto (City) v CUPE Local 79, 2003 SCC 63 at paras 37, 42, 51, 52 [CUPE]). SRFN’s position that Chief Heron remains suspended is contrary to the Court’s Judgment and an abuse of process.

propositions.text: SRFN's conduct warrants solicitor-client costs for this motion.
propositions.quote: SRFN’s conduct warrants costs of this motion on a solicitor-client basis.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant alleges SRFN abused process by continuing suspension and seeks solicitor-client costs.

propositions.text: Financial imbalance and forcing motion to return as Chief is extreme abuse of process.
propositions.quote: there is also a large financial imbalance between the parties. Forcing Chief Heron to file this motion so that she can simply return to her rightful role as Chief is an extreme abuse of process

propositions.text: Chief Heron is entitled to full solicitor-client costs.
propositions.quote: she is entitled to her full solicitor-client costs.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues financial imbalance and forced motion are abuse of process, entitling her to full solicitor-client costs.

propositions.text: If costs awarded, they should be to SRFN and against Chief Heron.
propositions.quote: If costs are awarded, the Court should award costs to SRFN and against Chief Heron.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues costs, if awarded, should go to SRFN against Chief Heron.

propositions.text: SRFN has not misused Court procedures or re-litigated matters before the Court.
propositions.quote: SRFN has not misused the Court’s procedures in any way that would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. SRFN is also not trying to re-litigate anything that was before the Court at the September 13, 2023 hearing

propositions.text: SRFN's only resort since March 12, 2024 was to file a Notice of Appeal, a proper review.
propositions.quote: SRFN’s only resort to the Court’s procedures since March 12, 2024 was to file a Notice of Appeal. As such, SRFN has brought a “proper review by way of appeal” (CUPE at para 52).

paragraphs.summary: Respondent denies misuse of procedures and says only proper appeal was filed after March 12, 2024.

propositions.text: SRFN denies Chief Heron was forced to file motion; Court granted her relief in Notices of Application.
propositions.quote: SRFN also denies that Chief Heron was “forced” to file this motion. The Court’s Judgment provides Chief Heron with the entirety of the relief she required in her Notices of Application.

propositions.text: SRFN acknowledged Court granted prohibition order on March 12, 2024.
propositions.quote: SRFN also acknowledged through its lawyers on March 12, 2024 that the Court granted the prohibition order.

propositions.text: Chief Heron filed motion despite Court's direction it is functus officio and to use Rule 397; motion wastes Court's time.
propositions.quote: Chief Heron brought this motion notwithstanding the Court’s direction on March 15, 2024 that it is functus officio and directing her to Rule 397. This motion is a waste of the Court’s time.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent denies forcing motion, notes Court granted relief, and says motion wastes Court time despite directions.

propositions.text: Applicant's motion is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the above reasons, the Applicant’s motion is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the applicant's motion.

propositions.text: Court exercises discretion to not award costs; each party bears own costs.
propositions.quote: I am exercising my discretion to not award costs of this motion to any party. Each party shall bear their own costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines to award costs and orders each party to bear their own costs.
